sections.这一篇讲什么:
**Evaluation answers one question: is this change better or worse than the last one?**
OpenAI defines a resilient prompt as
"one that provides high-quality responses across the full breadth of possible inputs".
Getting there takes evals, not feelings. The official path is the evaluation flywheel:
Analyze → Measure → Improve, round and round.
We have not run hands-on tests; the mechanisms below come from official tutorials and papers.
sections.第一步：人工看失败:
The flywheel starts with qualitative analysis: manually inspect and annotate failing examples.
The official cookbook gives a two-step annotation method:
open coding — read roughly 50 failing traces and attach descriptive labels to each error, discovery before taxonomy;
axial coding — group labels into higher-level categories to get a quantitative picture of the failure distribution.
Whichever category dominates is where improvement strikes first.

Why not jump straight to automatic metrics? The official answer is blunt:
metrics track progress but cannot reveal why a failure occurred.
Annotation turns scattered errors into an actionable roadmap.
sections.第二步：建自动评分器:
Turn failure modes into a test dataset and graders so measurement scales.
The OpenAI Evals cookbook splits grading in two:
code logic — string matching, JSON parseability; simple and reliable;
model grading — a model checks the answer against criteria, covering open-ended outputs.

The cookbook's example graders: a formatting grader checks the output shape,
and an accuracy grader compares against ground-truth columns in the dataset.
From then on, every change — new prompt, tuned parameters, new edge cases — gets a run.
The official advice is to wire graders into CI/CD and gate deployments on them.
sections.LLM 裁判与偏差:
Model grading scales, but the judge itself must be audited.
The paper systematically examines LLM-judge biases: position, verbosity, and self-enhancement,
plus limited reasoning ability. Strong judges can agree with human preferences at the level of human-human agreement (the paper's report).

The official cookbook gives a judge-calibration workflow:
use subject-matter-expert labels as the gold standard; test sets are usually imbalanced, so overall accuracy lies —
a judge that always says "pass" can score high while catching zero failures.
Watch both TPR (catching failures) and TNR (clearing passes).
Split the data three ways: a train set supplies few-shot examples for the judge prompt, a validation set tunes the judge,
and the test set runs once at the end to guard against overfitting.
sections.测试数据从哪来:
First choice: real inputs and outputs from production logs.
When data runs short, use synthetic data — but do not just say "generate N examples"; the official warning is that this produces homogeneity.
The structured approach: define key query dimensions (e.g., channel × intent × persona)
and generate across their combinations for broader coverage.
Then add perturbations: irrelevant information, deliberate mistakes, different slang — forcing edge behavior into the open.
sections.失败模式:
1. Prompt-and-pray: ship the change and hope. The official term for iteration without evals.
2. Uncalibrated judge: trusting scores without auditing the judge imports its biases and blind spots into your conclusions.
3. Test-set leakage: tuning the judge or the prompt on the test set makes the final score untrustworthy.
4. Pass-rate-only thinking: no idea where failures concentrate, so improvement has no priority.
5. Assuming the flywheel stops: fix the old failures and subtler new ones emerge — the cycle restarts.

The output of evaluation is not a score; it is a roadmap of what to change next.
